source.title: Mask2Shield: Strengthening LLM Safety against Neuron-Pruning Attacks
source.authors: Jin-Cheng Ying; Ming-Hui Xu; Yin-Hao Xiao; Xiu-Zhen Cheng; Wen-Cheng Yang

record.file_problem: Whole paper text is present; not garbled or cut off.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether selector-identified FFN-channel removal restores harmful compliance and reports that this vulnerability is substantially reduced after masked-forward training, refining the claim about safety being concentrated in a removable set.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the paper’s own pruning outcomes, ablations, and selected transfer results. Comparison results transcribed from SafeNeuron or TwinBreak are not treated as this study’s results. Capability benchmark results and the GSM8K refusal-keyword diagnostic do not measure the claimed harmful-compliance behavior. Selector statistics used to construct masks are not outcome rows.
record.test_reason: On Base instruction-tuned models, the study's own recomputed FFN-channel pruning restores harmful compliance, which bears directly on V5. It then shows that masked-forward training (M2S) removes this small removable safety set under the same and a second pruning pipeline. That qualifies V5 as a property of standard alignment rather than an inherent one.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that M2S reduces reliance on a small removable safety-neuron set: recomputed Safety-Neuron and TwinBreak pruning are far less effective, and aggressive pruning breaks coherent generation before restoring harmful compliance.
record.recipe_differences: The paper trains under functional FFN-channel masks with paired harmful refusal loss and benign teacher KL; it does not test the original fine-tuning intervention or response-token KL/prefill claims. It reports neuron-pruning attacks and a pruning-robustness defense.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies by model, pruning pipeline, and deletion ratio. The cumulative sweep uses HarmBench-13B CLS rather than the Llama-Guard judge used for the main and TwinBreak endpoints; at 10% targeted deletion, output validity falls to 0/313.
record.problems: The paper evaluates sparse channel deletion rather than unrestricted weight editing, retraining, or all white-box attacks. It says the mask depends on the NeuroStrike selector, uses full-parameter fine-tuning, and may require loss-weight searches for new model families. Main ASR uses 313 harmful prompts; the 10% sweep has no valid outputs, making its ASR uninterpretable as selective safety removal.
record.rows_left_out: The 60-row limit required omitting Table II TwinBreak JailbreakBench and StrongREJECT rows, TwinPrompt-100 values, and iterations 1–4; selected HarmBench and AdvBench endpoint rows are retained. Table IV no-KL ASR rows and the accompanying GSM8K keyword counts are also omitted. Cited comparison rows from SafeNeuron and published TwinBreak results are not this study’s measurements.

untested.parts: No per-token KL by response position.
No prefilling, suffix or decoding attacks.
Only selector-identified FFN gate/up channel zeroing is tested. Not tested: low-rank or other weight subsets, residual-direction ablation, unrestricted weight edits.
No analysis of why alignment is shallow (data or objective).
No positional deepening. M2S spreads safety across parameters, not response positions; its mask covers only the first 50 tokens, but positional depth is not measured.

record.verdict_notes: Several TwinBreak endpoint rows (II02, II03, II09) read the TP-100 column instead of Val; corrected above. rows_left_out says the Table IV no-KL ASR rows are omitted, yet IV10–IV12 are present. JailbreakBench and StrongREJECT TwinBreak panels are declared omitted and show the same pattern (M2S iteration-5 Val 0–6% vs published 84–95%). The cumulative sweep uses a different judge (HarmBench-13B CLS) from Table I (Llama-Guard-3-8B). M2S is a defense trained specifically against this pruning. Its rows therefore show that V5's localization is a contingent property of standard alignment, not that it never holds, so they are labelled limits_scope rather than challenges. Neither original source is this study.

versions.untested_parts: Fine-tuning on harmful examples to test harmful-request compliance without neuron pruning.
Ordinary or carefully selected benign fine-tuning and its effect on harmful compliance.
Per-token KL divergence by response position.
Prefilled openings, adversarial suffixes, and decoding changes.
The study tests selector-identified FFN-channel pruning, not whether all safety behaviour is localized in a few weights or ranks, or whether arbitrary weight edits have the same effect.
Whether data or training objectives cause first-token shallowness.
Whether safety training spreads behaviour across response positions beyond the first tokens and whether that positional change persists.
